utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. And good morning, everyone. For the record, all the accused except Borovcanin are present this morning. I take it, Mr. Lazarevic, that your client is unwell today and that waiver is on its way?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Yes, Your Honour is right. I spoke to Mr. Borovcanin earlier this morning. He informed me that he is not feeling well and he won't be able to attend this session. His waiver is on his way. He already signed it earlier this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. Representation, I see that for once all Defence teams -- no, there is Mr. Bourgon missing. There is Mr. Bourgon missing. The rest are present, Prosecution's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Good morning, General, I hope you had a good rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are going to continue this morning with the Gvero cross-examination and then we see who else and certainly with the Prosecution cross-examination. I estimate that you will be here for sure today and tomorrow with us, possibly, if not probably, also Wednesday. So, Mr. Josse -- or Mr. Krgovic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before we adjourned, we spoke about methods used to draft a directive. And let me ask you this: When it comes to the drafting of military documents, whether it's a complete or full method or a shortened method, as far as I can understand your testimony the role of operative organ is the same in both cases, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Irrespective of the chosen method of work, the role of all the organs of the command is the same in all the cases, not only of the operative organ. The role of all the organs is the same in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you passed your conclusions on the methods to be used in drafting the specific directive, you started from the assumption that the relationship in the command and the relationship between the military and political structures were harmonious, that there were no discords or discrepancies in opinion among the members of command. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I drafted my conclusions on the way the directive was drafted, I was governed primarily by the elements that impact the choice of the method for drafting a directive. These elements concerned the documents that is being drafted, which in this case is a directive, its strategic significance, its general implications for future periods, the available time that the command had at its disposal, i.e., the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska, and only later on I also looked at some mutual relationships and some possible ties between the relationships and their impact on the chosen method of work. And since in my expert report I did not mention this, it is my estimate that the relationships that prevailed and that fluctuated from good to bad did not have a significant impact on the choice of the method of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From the Miletic Defence, did you receive a document pointing to the fact that there were discords between General Milovanovic and the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received a number of documents, and primarily I mean that I got all the statements provided by General Milovanovic. I read all of them. I also read his publications, his views of the whole situation. I also had an occasion to see the transcript of his testimony provided here before the Tribunal. This had been translated for me. And I can say that the way I perceived the fluctuations and the relationships did not represent the problem that I was supposed to analyse in my expert report because I had never seen a -- too big a reflection on the process and methods of work. I saw particular aberrations of which I spoke in my testimony last week. I also saw some procedural discrepancies which I don't think had a major impact on the quality of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness please be shown 6D330.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a document -- this is a note by the security service, an official note. Look at the second paragraph. I am not interested in the part where it says that: "Only General Gvero was a good man in the General Staff," but the second part "... that General Milovanovic would be kicked out of the Main Staff." Were you privy to such information when drafting your expert report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I maybe ask that the witness read the whole sentence to the very end until -- up until the mention of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a problem with the witness reading the whole document. This is particularly why I told him that I was interested only in the -- in one part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But we are talking of seven lines, so let's not make a mountain out of a mole hill.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, no problem. I've read the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I had been privy to this document, which I wasn't, my opinion based on this document would have been something that is notorious, that is known. In strong hierarchical environments such as a military, it is generally known that there are several staffing policies or several ways to talk about the staff. One way is used by the subordinates, one way is used by the colleagues, and yet another way is used by the superior officers. One might say that this is a desirable outcome on the part of this major. This is what this major would like to see happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 6D312.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is another document issued by the security department. I am interested specifically in the third paragraph starting with the following words: "During the general conversation between our source and Vice-President Koljevic ..." Could you please read the paragraph very carefully. As you've just told us that there is a way that Mr. Koljevic, a member of the superior command, perceives relationships in the Main Staff where there are three streams: Hard-liner warriors with General Milovanovic; those who were willing to compromise, including General Gvero; and the third one that prefers Yugoslavia, including General Mladic. This document says that the relationships in the Supreme Command were not harmonious, at least from this angle. Would you agree with me when I say that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you. We have already discussed that when we were talking about the commence of orders. We said that there were problems, and this document dates from February 1995. We know that the political, military, and any other environment in the security sector was very volatile, that this was the year that was decisive, and we know that in any such situation there is a power struggle and the Army Republika Srpska was no exception to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about the directive. Did you have an occasion to read the part of the statement talking about the drafting of Directive 7 offered by General Milovanovic and General Skrbic who testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very important to repeat what I already said before this Trial Chamber last week. Before I got hold of some documents, I had already carried out a lot of research into the variations when it comes to the methods of work. And the method of work on the directive was something that General Milovanovic spoke about, and I was very confused when he said that there was an accompanying document signed. However, when all the pieces of the puzzle were revealed to me, and a very important piece of that puzzle in that process is Spreca from January to March and the command over the Spreca operation, and in the meantime, I received very good information about the dynamics of meetings with the president of Republika Srpska, then this confirmed that my conclusions about the methods of work were very probable, unlike any other methods on the methods of work used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Miletic's Defence show you General Djukic's statement about the method used to draft directives in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, but I would like my memory to be jogged on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have intention to show you the document, I just wanted to ask you whether you have had an occasion to see this statement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I am going to move on to another topic. When testifying before this Tribunal, you spoke about the establishment of the Main Staff, and I am going to ask you about the so-called personal establishment which was shown to you here. In 1992 when this personal establishment was determined, the same forms were used as in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army; is that correct? The same forms were used?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout the whole war -- or, rather, throughout the whole analysed period the same forms were used. Not only the same forms but also the same documents that define the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can understand your testimony before this Trial Chamber, the place in the establishment I -- determines the rank; am I correct when I think that? When you were talking about the columns?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm with you. Maybe this is a good moment for me to explain the meaning of the term "personal establishment," the meaning of "personal elements," and the meaning of "establishment elements" because this is a source of confusion very often. These terms are used in the professional part of the military and they are very often used in broader military circles, and then sometimes people are not familiar with the professional part and they are confused. The so-called personal establishment -- personnel establishment that was shown here and that I explained on the RF3 form implies part of the book that regulates the organisation and composition of manpower, because every establishment has a personnel part and the material part, and personnel part regulates what that person and that unit is entitled to with respect to materiel. As for the personal elements, those are the element that is every singular person has according to their rank. When the chief of operations and training at the beginning of his duty, General Miletic was colonel. That was his personal element. Establishment elements are the elements that the book envisages for the person with that rank. If the establishment elements are higher, then that person can be promoted in service; and if the establishment elements are the same, then there is no promotion. If the establishment elements are lower, this means that the posting is exceptional, but he will not be downgraded and the ranks will not be lowered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if you have a look in the case of a particular place or position, and we have a look at the establishment for that position, you can see the rank concerned, the duties that are performed, the position group, tasks -- or, rather, weapons issued, and the transport means used. That's what you have under establishment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What's missing, though, is the abbreviation VES, military specialty, which is what a person has to have in order to perform such duties. This is very important within military structures. It's decisive when it comes to appointing someone to a certain position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the VES, the position -- or, rather, the position group, well, as far as I have understood your testimony, this determines one's salary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position group, as I have said in my testimony -- or, rather, the rank group, influence all these matters. When we spoke about those who were seniors or juniors in the military, well, if you have two officers who have the same rank then the rank grouping defines who is senior, hence, the one who has a higher rank or higher rank grouping. This reflects the work that is performed, the value attributed to the work within that system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also said, 29978 of the transcript, that you didn't find any defined criteria according to which this rank grouping was done, if I have understood your testimony correctly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have understood my testimony correctly, but I was a little more precise. I said that unfortunately I didn't find any relevant documents such as a document that I often mention on organisational development. I didn't find those criteria, but I performed a detailed analysis of the establishments I came across, and I spoke to various individuals who worked on establishment issues in the army of the Republika Srpska, and I came to the conclusion that criteria were used for defining establishment elements, criterion that were in accordance with those used by the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To be specific, with regard to rank groupings, if a -- if an officer in accordance with JNA rules receives the grade twice, that he excels, he has a rank grouping that is one level higher regardless of his position and his rank; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be precise, you are right. If an officer has a rank grouping that is identical to the establishment group, and if he then twice gets the grade excels, then he has a rank grouping that is one level higher or one level higher than the establishment group. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So is it possible for a corps officer to have the same rank grouping as an officer in the Main Staff, for example, group 3?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you analyse the criterion in a little more detail, the criteria according to which I identified rank, and these are documents that every army in the world has, these are important documents because they form the basis for structuring protocol and other such matters, in that case you must have noticed that in the Republika Srpska Army, the corps commanders were very high-ranking. Or, rather, I pointed this out because corps commanders and corps officers frequently had higher rank groupings than officers in the Main Staff because their position and their importance was evaluated to be of much importance for the system. So it's not just because of the grade excellent or excels, but the system is such that some corps officers have higher positions that many -- than many officers in the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army, and this is the case worldwide not just in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So what is the importance of the rank group then if an officer in the corps has group 3 and an officer in the main corps has a rank grouping 3? What is the relationship when it comes to rank?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the answer to what I said with regard to rank and order. First you establish the rank, it's clearly defined, and you can see this from the definition that I have provided. And when you deal with rank -- well, rank groups are important only within that rank. It's just a matter of whether he's the first, second, third, or fourth. Perhaps an officer who has a third rank has a higher rank grouping than someone in the second rank, but he can't be senior to him because he's not of that rank. So it's not said in vain when you say that there is a rank and order within a given rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned criteria that defined rank groupings, General, I had a detailed look at what you called the working map of the personnel development, and I saw rank grouping 3. Within that group, apart from Commander Mladic, all generals -- all those who had the rank of General in the JNA had that rank grouping, those who became members of the Army Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would my colleague please submit the document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's for me to decide on the order of my questions and when I will show the witness documents. I am laying the basis for my question, and I will choose the appropriate time to show the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... understand but I am not absolutely certain that Commander Mladic was in fact part of group 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will need to see the document in any case, so let's bring out this document and put it on the ELMO or on e-court if it is available on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you have a detailed look at this excerpt from the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, this working map that contains names, that lists certain names?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the following document, P3178.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak into the microphone or speak a little more loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, who exactly needs to speak --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel for the Defence is kindly asked to speak a little more loudly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters are having a little bit of a problem because they think you are not speaking near enough -- near your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, have a look at the first page of this establishment document. We have General Mladic's name as commander. He has been assigned rank grouping 2. Could we have a look at the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge first paragraph, first part of the front page, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that the rank he is assigned is 02.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at the following page of the document, please. Could we have a look at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And here you can see that in the case of General Milovanovic -- well, the General has a rank grouping 3.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now -- just a minute please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 05057629 is the ERN number. I apologise, 35, it's 35. You can't see the ERN number very clearly in my copy. 7635. Could you scroll down a bit, please. That's not the page. The following page, please. It's page 11 in the e-court system. Just a little lower down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's the rank grouping of General Gvero, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, let's have a look at page that deals with the logistics sector. I have a different copy here, 7637. Page 13 in the e-court system. Could you scroll down a bit, please. Scroll down a little more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is General Djukic, and can you see that his rank grouping is 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now let's have a look at page 7658. The ERN number is 7658.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps rank grouping for General Talic is 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I am not absolutely certain where my colleague sees "3," I can read "4" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the column under lieutenant-colonel's VES 3109903. It's below that. It's the third column from the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, apart from General Mladic who was a General in the JNA army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that now, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. It's just that I was slightly confused because there was a position group also that indicates 04, so maybe the witness could tell us a little more about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic and General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, apart from General Mladic, as far as I know according to the first-hand information I received, only four other officers had the rank of General in the JNA, and they were Milovanovic, Djukic, Gvero, and Talic. That was in 1992. And they had rank groupings in accordance with this fact. Would you agree with my assessment?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood the question, and the question was whether I agree that the establishment in the Army of Republika Srpska was done in accordance with the rank that the persons that you just mentioned had in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was the criterion when their rank grouping was determined, i.e., that the establishment was actually drafted to accommodate the persons.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't agree with you. The establishment that was drafted and that was carried out here, and I had an occasion to talk to the people who were very important professional consultants, and they were consulted when this establishment was done, it is a very hierarchical establishment that provided for subordination, and it was developmental because it provided for the people who were brought to these establishment positions as officers to be promoted in their rank. Judging by the example that we just saw, and we saw two group -- four -- five ranking groups, we saw that four officers, Milovanovic, Djukic, Gvero, and Mladic had the same personal establishment elements and personnel elements. And this is not a surprise. These are the highest ranking officers. And we saw that a commander of the 1st Krajina Corps had the personnel establishment 3 -- 4, and the rank grouping 3, which means that he was able to promote and that the elements could be raised after he had spent some time in that position and when his assessment was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General Talic was standing in for General Mladic that position after all; isn't that correct? The Chief of the Main Staff, that is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very important element in the rank and ranking that I spoke about. I did not emphasize this in the organisation and establishment. When I said that standing in is a temporary situation, that it isn't necessarily evil for a short period of time, without much authority and powers, and lasts only until the moment a decision is brought about acting on behalf of somebody. When we were talking about different variants and when we were talking about on who would be representing the commander or the Chief of Staff who are not there, they were preventing for performing their duties, what you just told is an essential issue. If the commander and the Chief of Staff had been prevented in performing their duties, it would probably be the president of the republic who would issue a decision for them to be represented by one of the corps commanders, and it would probably be the commander of the 1st Corps. This is a very essential essence of the difference between representing, standing in for, and acting, and what elements arise from the representing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just a correction my question. I asked you this, after all General Talic replaced General Mladic in his position, he was his successor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no succession in the army. After all, at one point he was appointed the commander of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska. That is the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, one more question. The authorities and powers of the officers or military personnel are not determined by the establishment but by the rules on authorities and powers. Wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The establishment is a very important document that is involved in determining the role and place of somebody in the system, together with many other documents, and this also determines what he, that person, could, should, and had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: However, the powers and authorities are established by other documents, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are established by the law and this order on the authorities of the organisational units. These are the regulations that govern this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, these are the rules of the JNA such as the rules of the authorities of the land army in peacetime and rules of the authorities on the military district in peacetime. These are the regulations that regulate this matter. Would I not be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule on authorities and powers regulated was the governing document until 1993. After that, the rule was replaced by the order. These two documents regulated the authorities and powers for the specific organisational units. The one that you mentioned was the rule of the authorities of officers in the land army, that's one document, and the other one on military districts is different, and they cannot be applied to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska because we are talking about two different organisational units and all of their elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So what rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, one moment, because I get the feeling from the interpreter's voice that we are going too fast. We are going too fast. She is doing a tremendous job in trying to catch up with both of you, but I don't think we will keep it that way. So slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which rule would regulate this matter in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be or there should have been a rule on the authorities of the organisational units of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska or an order on the authorities and powers of the organisational units of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska; or if these two documents did not exist because of the analogy that they used, what must have been used was the order on the authorities of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. One of these documents must have had a direct or indirect impact on looking at the authorities and powers of all the organisational units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: However, did you not see these documents or -- and you did not use them in the drafting of your expert report; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rule and order on authorities and powers of the organisational units of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia I did use pertaining to that period, and I analysed some things that were done, and I can conclude that either the experience of the officers who were members of the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska or the rule in a small number of copies was something that was directly or indirect used. And as for the two documents that you have mentioned and that the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska should have had, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And very concretely now, as far as I can understand from your CV, you were not a member of the Army Republika Srpska, and you do not have personal first-hand knowledge on how the hierarchical relationship functioned in the Army Republika Srpska. The officers of the Main Staff and people who were directly involved in the Army of Republika Srpska are better suited to tell us something about that; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that I was never a member of the Army of Republika Srpska. It is also true that I am not contesting the competencies and authorities of any of the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska. However, it is also true that I developed as an expert on the organisation and command and that I had contacts with my colleagues who were involved in that matters in the Army of Republika Srpska. We discussed the matters extensively. I often proposed my own positions with that regard, and as an expert I tried hard to study the matters as best as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P410. Could the Court please produce page 7, Article 10. Article 10, please. Page 8 in the English version, please. In the Serbian version, Article 10, page 7, please. I apologise, it is page 10. In my copy it is page 7 so could -- can we see the following page, please, the one ending with ERN numbers 47065.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC

If the commander and the Chief of Staff are both absent at the same time, the commander shall be replaced by the officer assigned on the order of the commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit 6D36 -- 336. Unfortunately, Your Honours, we do not have the translation of this document. I am going to ask the witness to read Article 10 of the document -- or the rules, rather. Although it is the same as Article 10 in the previous rules. 6D336. The last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you on the screen because I have something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am talking about Exhibit 6D336.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree with me that the contents of this article are the same as the contents of the same article in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I can see only Article 10, I would suppose that this document is the Rules on Responsibilities and Powers of a Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 1 of the same document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No need to do that because I recognise the document anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that the two documents treat representation of a commander in an identical way?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree with you in that. However, I believe, Your Honours, that we need some very important explanation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I will come to that. I apologise. I just want to ask you something else, and I will go back to this topic later on. I just wanted to establish that one fact. I wanted to ask you whether the two documents treat the matter in the -- in an identical way. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text is identical, however, we are talking about different levels and we will be discussing the two levels later, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of January you testified on page 3022 on line 8, and -- I apologise, 30022, 30022 is the page number, and you spoke about command posts. You said then that there is just one command post which consists of several elements, and then you said that one of the elements is the basic command post. The second element is a forward command post, and you also spoke about the system of command posts. You spoke about that based on a rule. What rule is it that determines the elements of a command post?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I retain the right, Your Honours, to say something about the previous thing in detail because the definition that this is identical is not acceptable. And when I spoke about command posts, I was answering a question, and the question was whether somebody was something this or the other in a command post, and then I said that a command post per se does not mean a thing, that there is a system of command posts and that there are several command posts; the basic command posts, the forward command post, the force command post, a reserve command post, and so on and so forth. In general terms when we are talking about command posts and the system of command posts, we have to consult rules of combat, we have to consult professional literature, military lexicon, military encyclopedias, and in principles these are all guiding documents. They are mostly never conflicting, and I adhere to that fact. And I repeat that if you take the most applicable rule about the work of the commands, I would like to repeat that this is a system of command posts because under chapter Command Posts there is an explanation of all these command posts that may be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P699. Page -- these are instructions for the work and operations staff, page 31 in the Serbian and Croatian language, or, rather, in the Serbian language, and page 27 -- or, rather, I apologise. In the English version it's page 31. It's page 31 in both the Serbian and English version -- or, rather, in the e-court system it's page 33. I apologise. The page I have in the B/C/S version doesn't correspond to the one in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What confuses me is that you mentioned the elements of command post whereas here the elements explains in a somewhat different manner. Here it says that the main elements are the command group, the auxiliary group, and the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under 51 you can see exactly what I said. The main command post, not the command post, but the main command posts consists of a command group, an auxiliary group, and a communications centre, and that's what I was saying about the system of command posts. The forward command post is different way -- is organised in a different way, rear command post is organised in a different way, but all together they constitute a system, the purpose of which is to exercise command pursuant to the authority of the organisational unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the following document, chapter 3 on command posts. The ERN number is 239389, and in the English version it's page 27. It's page 27 in the e-court system in the B/C/S version. 29 in the e-court system, I apologise. The ERN number in the English version is 11626.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I assume you've seen this document on numerous occasions. What I am interested in is the following, the part that deals with rear command posts or logistics command posts which says that rear command posts can take over the role of main command posts if it's impossible to command from the command post. To control, to exercise command and control from the command post. Do you agree with me that that's what it says in these instructions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony before this Court, you said that if the Commander-in-Chief were not at the command post, in that case the most senior officer would be the assistant for morale and religious issues. That's what you said. And you said that that is what arises from the establishment structure; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was the context, but I wasn't that precise. I probably said who was the most senior person at the command post. I probably mentioned the matter of seniority. It's important to point out that if the commander isn't at the command post, he's still in command of the unit. That's something that's very important, in my opinion. But what is very important in this case, in the case of the command post, and you can see this in -- or under item 43 that's on the screen and also under item 44. My explanation was based on everything I have said, but what is important is something that we really must bear in mind. What are the purposes of the instructions? Let me just emphasize one issue. These instructions were drafted when the information organ was in the staff, the intelligence organ was in the staff, and then the command -- the command's work or the staff's work was organised in a certain manner. The Army of Republika Srpska had an intelligence and security sector that had been organised in a particular manner, and with regard to that aspect, these instructions can't be applied literally when analysing the Army of Republika Srpska. You have to analyse them in a creative manner. It's not just enough to have a look at what is written here. Since the Main Staff of the Army Republika Srpska wasn't well manned, wasn't fully manned, the way it was organised and the way it worked was very specific as a result of this lack of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is something I wanted to ask you about. You expressed your opinion on who the most senior officer was when the commander was not present or when the deputy commander wasn't present, but did you consult any officers from Republika Srpska? Didn't the Miletic Defence provide you with testimony of some officers from the Main Staff who addressed this matter, because, General, the rules are one thing and the situation on the ground, real life, wartime situations, that's another thing; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We fully agree on that. However, the question you have put is very problematic. If the commander and the Chief of Staff are not in the staff, well, who replaces the commander? If the commander and Chief of Staff are not at the basic command post, who replaces the commander? Very often you don't have a sign of identity between two solutions. Perhaps I provided certain models as an answer. This was then a very precise solution, a precise model, and then on the basis of that model I said who should replace such a commander, but in practice things can be different. I didn't deal with this matter because I had no way in which to come to such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Miletic Defence, when proofing you, show you Milomir Savcic's. He's testified before this Court and he in fact addressed the question of how things weren't in practice. General Savcic is an officer -- or was an officer from the Main Staff. He later became the chief of the intelligence department and had a high rank in the Main Staff. Have you had the opportunity of examining his testimony with regard to this matter?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had the opportunity of reading through his statement. I have been through almost all the testimonies, and on the whole I focused on testimony that specifically related to the issues I was to deal with. If there is anything specific or concrete I would like to see it, and I would be glad to make a professional contribution to the matter, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'll read out General Savcic's testimony. He testified before the Court, page 15322 and it ends at 15323. The Miletic Defence examined General Savcic about the matter we are dealing with -- well, I will tell you what he said: "[In English] Yes, that's the general rule. If a commander or some other senior officer is unable to discharge his duty, then another person will replace him as is provided by the establishment rules." [Interpretation] And then the Miletic Defence continues to examine the witness: "[In English] In principle ..." [Interpretation] This was the answer to the question as to whether it was the general rule. And then General Savcic continues, and I'll read it out in English: "[In English] In principle this can be regulated in two ways. One way is for the commander to decide a senior officer who would replace him while he's absent if we are dealing with a shorter period of time. And then there is an unwritten rule, especially during war, that when the commander is absent, and when his deputy is absent, the assistant commander for logistics serves as the most senior officer. This is done for a very practical reason. When the command post is developed within the combat order, it has at least two elements: It serves as the basic command post where the command group is located headed by the commander, Chief of Staff and the entire staff. And then, in the logistic command post, which is separated, it's detached, they are not next to each other, there is the assistant commander for logistic together with his logistic organ and chief of various organ -- together with his logistic organ and chief of various services -- together with his logistic organ and chiefs of various services. "The security organ and the organ for moral guidance, religious and legal affairs, can be located either -- in either of two command posts since combat operation inevitably incur losses should the command post is destroyed, should the command group be neutralised, this is the mechanism that was developed mainly for the assistant commander for logistic to take over as the most senior officer." [Interpretation] General, are there any reasons for which you would doubt that General Savcic did not tell the truth when he testified about this subject before the Court?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I said I had any doubts it would be a catastrophe in terms of military culture if someone had not spoken the truth. So what I have said, well, now is the best time to be more precise. At one point in time I said that I agreed with something that General Savcic said. He mentioned the system of standing in for someone else. He was very precise. He mentioned a method that consists of the following: When a commander designates who will stand in for him, but he is not present and nor is the Chief of Staff. In my work I analysed two methods. The first one is the method that is implemented automatically. If the commander and the Chief of Staff leave, then in certain situations the person that will stand in for the commander is dealt with automatically. This is the most senior person as stated in the Rules of Service, and this was also the case in the rules on the Army of Republika Srpska later on. At this point in time, as I have said, the practice in certain situations that General Savcic has addressed was as follows. The practice was based on all of the rules that were in force. The commander, when absent, could designate someone to stand in for him. He could designate any of his assistants. They were on an absolutely equal footing, and the reason for which he opted for the assistant commander for logistics was quite logical. General Savcic was quite right with regard to this model. I spoke about the automatic process in the case of another model, and we were both compatible with each other, and this is great for this Court and for the profession that we are both involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will have another half-hour, but if we can take our break now because I am going to move on to another topic, and I would like to structure my questioning for after the break, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Krgovic. We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I interrupted you as you were explaining the difference between the corps and the military district. So would you please tell us what it was that you intended to explain.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Basically, these two rules are almost identical as far as these points are concerned, but they actually are different because they treat two different commands of a different level, a different structure, and having different tasks. However, these two articles are almost identically worded because both refer to the rule of standing in and the appointment of a stand-in officer. However, both the documents when they refer to standing-in representation actually do not say that Article 10 is sufficient for such standing in to indeed examination. Both articles are based on the law and it accentuates that this actually -- this appointment, stand-in appointment begins under an order on standing in and starts running as of that -- the issuance of such an order. So this is not an automatic process. Both these rules, however, are of course in compliance with the law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day of your testimony you said -- actually, you discussed rank and sequence, and you gave us a diagram, a map, rather, which you drew as a supplement to your expert work in which you sequence these posts or put them in a specific order. On the 12th of January, on page 29991: "[In English] The document concerning the rank ..." [Interpretation] It is page 29991. "[In English] The document concerning the rank and the order of commanding officers in an army is something that almost every army in the world should have." [Interpretation] And as far as I could gather, as far as I could understand this diagram or whatever we shall call it, this sequence that you gave, this is not contained in any rule or any document but it was you, yourself, who made it on the basis of your perception of the establishment structure; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not exist as a model, rank and order, not as a model defined under any specific rule. However, the rules of service and the laws which deal with the levels of subordination and superiority, of seniority and junior positions, those which refer to subordination and to hierarchy as well as protocols which are of the essence for the unfolding of specific activities of almost -- require of almost all commands to have this document in one way or another. I use that methodology in order to send a message regarding appointment, substitution, standing in, et cetera, in order to show this perception of a military organisation and military hierarchy so that this document was produced -- or, rather, this drawing number 14, figure number 14 in my expert work, in my expert report, was made inter alia on the basis of the establishment structure, the establishment structure of subordinated units. And as there is no document found which is called the Organisational Development so as to explain what this looks like an importance source for this are directives from which the order of the units was extracted as given in those directives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were drawing this other figure where you were marking the order of the different organs, you started with the staff and the Chief of Staff, you marked General Jovanovic [as interpreted] with a number 1. If we are talking about the level of the Army of Republika Srpska -- excuse me, it is Milovanovic. It is misspelled in the transcript. So Milovanovic is marked by you with number 1 as, actually, the commander is the one who should be marked by number 1. What do you have to say to that? I can show it to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem. I have understood your question perfectly. I know what you are talking about. Here I was shown the organisational chart of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, although I had had occasion to see it in the expert report of the expert Mr. Butler, and to which I raised a number of objections and I stated my argumentation substantiating my objections. The order or the sequence in this chart which I showed does not refer to persons, not to Milovanovic. It is the order of organisational units of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, the first organisational level, and that is the order which is extracted from the establishment structure book. And the establishment book has to be made in keeping with the organisational development or structure of the Army of Republika Srpska. So this is the order given at that level. It is not at that level that we have the commander, and the end of that process is the planning of development and finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And further in your work you explained the levels of command. I have to admit that bearing in mind what you stated before in terms of the unity of command where the right of command is exclusively in the competence of the commander and the part where you refer to strategic and operational levels of command, I must admit that that level of command in the Main Staff is something that I don't exactly understand. These can be levels of hierarchy or of subordination, but the right of command is vested in the commander solely; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The right of commanding with the Army of Republika Srpska is the right of the commander, but the entire structure, the entire -- an entire cluster of other participants also are vested with the right of command within their respective spheres of competence. When we are talking about the strategic, operational, and tactical levels of command, I was referring to the Army of Republika Srpska, and there are no dilemmas whatsoever and there we completely agree. When we talk about the Main Staff and in the Main Staff it's -- and in the Main Staff itself, as a sub-system of this large system, you have different levels of command. You have the first level of command where we have organisational units of sector rank, and they are ordered in one colour and the one order of magnitude. Then you have the second level where we have organisational units of administration levels, and the certain departments they have a different colour. Then there is the third level of command with organisational units where the organisational units are of the rank of sections, mainly. So I was very precise when I said what levels of command I was referring to. The first -- the one level was in the command level, Main Staff level, and the others in the other two which I -- three which I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a work of authorship by you. This is not something which is envisaged in any rules of command ordered or described, laid out the way you did it? At least I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, this is not a work of authorship or sensibility or perception on the part of the author himself as such. This is a methodolgy which deals with organisation. In each organisation a structure can be ordered by levels on the basis of certain specific rules; hence, this methodolgy which is shown here has been processed in both specialised papers, in rules, and in books, and in some specialised papers the authors have actually cited a number of experts who have used these papers and these levels as I have put them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to these documents, in regard of establishment, another order has been shown or a sequence, arrangement of organs in the Main Staff, how they were ordered according to rank and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can Exhibit 6D333 please be uploaded and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, we have this document only in the Serbian language, but I am not interested in its content. Please look at this number, the reference number which is 01.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: 01. That is General Ratko Mladic's number as the commander of the Main Staff. His number was 1, 01. Although he could sign documents also produced by other organs so that you will see his signature in other documents also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit 5D975, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the reference number on top, which is 02.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You see it is General Manojlo Milovanovic. We will see his signature on other documents as well, but these are documents from the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit 5D1016, please. Can we go to the right-hand side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is already indisputable that number 03, which we see in the reference number, is the number of the operations organ -- operations and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit 5 -- P, sorry, P2516. P2516.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is 07. That is the reference number of the sector for morale, religious and legal affairs. General, is it not possible that the rank and the order of the organs in the Main Staff was somewhat different than what is given in your own schedule? Is it not that Mladic is number 1 in the Main Staff of the VRS, Milovanovic 02, and General Miletic 03, namely third in rank or literally the third man in the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only is this not possible but this is a general confusion of the issue. The reference number in the reference book in the registry book does not define by any document whatsoever what 01, 02, or 03 refers to. This is most often defined by the office administrator, by the chief of the office either according to his own design and assignment of numbers or according to the receipt of documents. Mainly, and as a rule, the chiefs do not interfere with that office and with the assignment of reference numbers as such. Their reference numbers often refer to the frequency of the incoming and outgoing documents. From the aspect of organisation and the organising of that process, the reference number has nothing whatsoever to do in terms of cause or effect with rank and order. The reference number's sole purpose is to -- for you to be able to locate a document in that book. It is an arbitrary number. It is assigned by the acting chief who actually is not in charge or versed in the organisation of the system. He's only versed with his only organisation of that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So 01, 02, 03, does that refer to the organisational units in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because this reference number follows.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat. The reference number is an arbitrarily assigned number assigned to a unit under which it will be able to identify its document. Responsible for the assignment of the reference number is the head of the office. The criterion applied by the head of the office is something that only he may be able aware of. It can refer to the frequency of correspondence. It can be based on anything else. The rank and order are kept in the sector for organisational, communicational, and personnel affairs. These are documents which define rank and order from strictly confidential to state secret, and documents as such are not actually passed to the office for them to define what number to assign it because this is office work and that is quite something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in determining rank and order did you have an occasion to talk to the officer of the Republika Srpska, did you talk to Colonel Dragoljub Keserovic [as interpreted] as well? He was an officer in the Main Staff, an officer in charge of security there.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to Keserovic, but I did talk to the competent Colonel, Colonel Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Miletic Defence show you the testimony provided by a Colonel Keserovic in the Blagojevic case? He spoke precisely on the same topic on which you provided your expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't show me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to read one part of the transcript, and then I will ask for your comment on that part. This is on page 1071 on 10 June, 2004. My learned friend Mr. McCloskey questioned Colonel Blagojevic [as interpreted], and he asked him the following -- Colonel Keserovic. And the page number 10701. My learned colleague McCloskey asked Colonel Keserovic as follows: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... 17th, 18th, who was basically in charge over there when Mladic wasn't around?" [Interpretation] The answer is this: "[In English] I really don't know who was the most senior ranking officer as the operation officer. He would be the number three man on the staff." [Interpretation] And now I have to read once again since -- "Q. [In English] 16, 17, 8 -- 18th, who was basically in charge over there when Mladic wasn't around? "A. I really don't know. Miletic -- Miletic was the most senior ranking" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Two things. I want to know if interpretation in B/C/S is being received. That's number one. And secondly the transcript stopped -- but it's not on mine. Yes, yes, okay. It seems to be okay on one monitor but not on the -- not on the other one. We are not receiving transcript, in other words, on the LiveNote. Well, that would be my preference but I have to see whether everyone is in agreement. Position is as follows: The transcript is rolling on the monitor, on the monitor, but it's not on the LiveNote. Options are we stop until we fix this or if there is agreement we can proceed and then the missing ... As far as I am concerned we could proceed, but I want to make sure everyone else agrees. And on previous occasions we have had requests from some Defence teams insisting that they needed the LiveNote to be functioning, too, before we could proceed. So that's what I want to make sure of. All right. I see no objections. Basically, then, let's proceed. I just want to make sure that whatever you have read in English has been translated into B/C/S. Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- then let's proceed, and in the meantime we try to fix this technical hitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to repeat the answer: "[In English] I really don't know. Miletic was the most senior-ranking officer as the operations officer -- as the operations officer. He would be the number three man on the staff." [Interpretation] And further on, page 10707, it says -- Judge Argibay asks Colonel Keserovic about the same topic the following. Keserovic. The question was as follows: "[In English] You told us that General Tolimir was the number 4 in the Main Staff, that General Miletic was number 3, and we all know that General Mladic was number 1. But I am not sure from the transcript this morning, or yesterday, when you were talking about General Milovanovic, was he number 2 in the Main Staff? [Interpretation] And the answer: "[In English] Your Honour, General Milovanovic was the number 2. Milovanovic, but General Tolimir was not number 4." [Interpretation] And further on, a bit later, Judge Argibay asks: "[In English] Could you give me more or less the order, then. More or less." [Interpretation] The answer: "[In English] For the first three, what you said is quite right. Mladic, Milovanovic, and then Miletic. And then the assistants, according to their departments, come in the following: Tolimir, Gvero, Djukic, Tomic. I think those were the sectors represented at the time." [Interpretation] And then I will take you back to the previous answer which concerns Tolimir. "[In English][Previous translation continues] ... Tolimir was probably number 4 -- was number 4." "I really don't remember saying that. I think I didn't give a number. He is one of the assistant commanders of the Main Staff, and there were five or six then at the same level -- on the same level in the hierarchy." General, do you have any reason to doubt Colonel Keserovic's words? Do you think that he was not telling the truth when he was talking about his specific knowledge as an officer of the Main Staff and he was talking about the rank and order of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am interested in is what duties did Colonel Keserovic discharge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He was the security officer in the Main Staff, later on in the General Staff and a full-time professor at the security academy.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about factual things here, not about --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It arises from everything I've been interpreted from the transcript, and from my point of view it -- being an expert for organisation, and based on that I enjoy my status and rank, Colonel Keserovic should have put a full stop after the first sentence, which was "I don't know ..." Everything he said after that just confirmed his first sentence, "I don't know." I would really love to see anybody in the world show me a single military where an officer, a colonel or a major-general comes before a commander [as interpreted] with a lieutenant-general or similar rank. The fact that in accordance with what you read out to me, he forgot very important assistant commander, the assistant for organisation, mobilization, and personnel matters, and that he was talking about military and forgot corps commanders, that he did not give you the basis for his ranking and order, then I can only assume that he believes that the Army of Republika Srpska was an -- anarchic, lacked organisation, and that there was a grab for ranks and other things. Based on all the documents that I studied, there was no anarchy, there was no grab for ranks, and the order was well known. This is based on nothing, and especially not on the principles of organisation, hierarchy, and subordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a quick correction of the transcript at line 13 on page 39. It should be before the assistant commander, "assistant commander" is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So it would read: "I would really love to see anybody in the world show me a single military where an officer, Colonel or Major-General comes before the assistant commander," is that correct, "with a lieutenant-general of similar rank." Is this what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony on page 29984, to General Miletic's Defence question you said that such a possibility does exist, but within your view it is not likely. If you wish me I can read back to what you said. You said that it was a likely possibility.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read it back to me. I never had such a view of the Army of Republika Srpska, especially after having studied so many documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is your testimony on 12th January, 2009, page number 29984, line 6. And the question is this: "[In English] Could General Miletic have been the senior officer in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska in a given circumstance?" "There is a possibility and there is a model that he could have been seen as the most senior officer in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the -- my learned colleague read the answer to the very end, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend can do it in her additional examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't indeed because that would completely alter the meaning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the rest of the paragraph relevant to what was asked to the witness in the first place or not? I think you need to explain this first.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told the witness that he confirmed the whole thing, but he said that it was not very likely. That's why I did not want to read the rest of this answer because in my question I already addressed the possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But let's take it in a logical sequence. If you look at page 40, line 14, when you were putting the question to the witness you asked him as follows: "In your testimony on page 28894 to General Miletic's Defence question, you said that, 'Such a possibility does exist, but within your view it is not likely.' If you wish me I can read what you -- read to what you said." "'You said that it was a likely possibility?'" And then the witness told you: "Yes, please read it out to me. I never had such a view of the Army of Republika Srpska, especially after having studied so many documents." And then you started reading. The second paragraph, which we have here, says: "There is a possibility and there is a model that he could have seen as the most senior officer in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska." To me it is obvious that this is not complete. In other words, he must have followed up with something to explain his position so that we can understand what he said then and now better. So I suggest that you read out the next part that there is, provided it is relevant to what we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So your answer: "[In English] There is a possibility and there is a model that he could have been seen as the most senior officer in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, General Miletic or the Head of Administration for Teaching and Operation, but this would be, as it were, a headless model or a pointless model."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible that General Miletic was the most senior officer as General Keserovic said in his testimony before this Court? Colonel Keserovic was in the Main Staff. You weren't.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive a mandate from this Court to be an expert with regard to whether I was in the Main Staff or not. My assignment as an expert was to address certain issues on the basis of documents. And on the basis of my experience and my education and on the basis of the duties that I performed. This was the task that I had to perform. So I have stated and I have provided all the arguments that nothing said apart from the first sentence is correct, as far as organisation is concerned, that refers to Colonel Keserovic's statement. He certainly is a great security officer, but as far as organisational matters are concerned, I categorically claimed he doesn't know anything about them. What I said on the first day is something that I stand by today, too. That would have meant that the RS army didn't have a commander, didn't have a single assistant commander, didn't have a single corps commander, a single Chief of Staff in the corps, and then General Miletic, given his rank and educational level, would have been the first man. But in such an organisational structure -- well, an army without such a system is senseless. It's not just a matter of saying that it would act in a senseless manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to doubt that Colonel Keserovic committed perjury when testifying here. He was expressing his own impression. He expressed his opinion. He wasn't testifying in his capacity as an expert. That's what he thought about the way the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army functioned.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was very precise. At no time did it occur to me to say that a witness to whom I had no spoken was lying or not lying, but I was very precise when I said that what he explained was something he didn't know anything about. And he himself said he didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that Mr. Keserovic was on the list of witnesses for the Miletic Defence and he was supposed to testify immediately after you, and then he was suddenly withdrawn so as to not testify in this case. Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you answer, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what my learned colleague is saying is not exactly right. I think we all know why Mr. Koserovic could not come and give his testimony, quite simply because he did not get his visa, and my learned colleague could always call him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, what's the relevance of the question, Mr. Krgovic? Let's move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Haynes, do you still require about 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I should think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would be obliged if Mr. Krgovic could just hand me the lectern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, good morning, General Kosovac.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I represent Vinko Pandurevic who, in July of 1995, was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just a couple of preliminary questions to get us down from Main Staff levels of command. He was at that time a lieutenant-colonel. Can you confirm that that is an inferior rank to a colonel?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to follow the logic down of figure 14 to your report, if, as you opined, the operations officer at the Main Staff level was at rank level 6, it would follow, wouldn't it, that a brigade commander was at rank level 10?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That kind of rank and order is not drawn up for the whole army because there is no relation of cause and effect. With the rank of operations officer, well, he would be at the first or second organisational level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we will move on. I am not going to waste time going through, as it were, how we go down from the bottom of your existing figure. I take it you would agree with me that in relation to the Yugoslav National Army, a vast number of documents were produced to regulate the way in which it operated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since the -- a lot of documents that refer to organisation defined how things were to be organised, some of those documents were adopted by the Army of Yugoslavia. They weren't redrafted. I'm talking about these specific documents that pertain to organisation. Part of the documents were supplemented, and the Army of Republika Srpska took over most of the documents that the Army of Yugoslavia was already using, at the least the documents that had to do with the subject of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And those documents had varying degrees of legal status. Some of the them, for example, had the force of law. Some of them were regulatory. Some of them were merely for guidance. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree with that absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like us to look now at one such document, and I know straight away it's not a document that you look at in preparation of your report, but I hope that doesn't disadvantage you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's firstly P408. And it would be helpful if we could have in e-court page 1 in B/C/S for the witness and the Serb speakers and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Kosovac, is that big enough for you to read on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to focus your attention on the very top of the document. You can read it in your own language, but it is headed "Federal Secretariat for National Defence, JNA General Staff, Infantry Administration." Are you familiar with that body, the Infantry Administration of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Infantry of the Main Staff of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, I am familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just in a sentence or two, what was it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the General Staff of the JNA, the administrations for services and departments were organised in different ways and these administrations for services and departments are either grouped as sectors or they were independent, but their main task was to develop their services and arms and this included the field of drafting rules for the units of specific services and combat arms. For a while I was a junior officer in the airforce and anti-aircraft defence sector and I was responsible for dealing with anti-aircraft defence, so I was very familiar with this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
