utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go down now a little bit on the front page. We see that this document is dated the 20th of July, 1984, and then the authority of the document is set out. It says: "Pursuant to item 34c of the instructions on the preparation and use of professional military literature, I hereby proscribe the following ..." In terms of legal force, what legal force does an instruction have?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These rules and instructions were guiding. They are not binding. They are guide-lines and they serve as a basis so the individuals can attain the objectives assigned to them in the best possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very helpful. Now, I want to move on please to another version of the same document which is more fully translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd like to look, please, at P694. In the English we will need to see page 3, and in the B/C/S for the witness we will have to look at pages 12 and 13, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, General Kosovac, as I've said, I know you didn't study this document in preparation of your report because you weren't talking about brigades in your report. So please take your time to read that page and then the next page of the document in your language and let us know when you have finished.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can go on to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks very much. What we looked at previously was, as it were, the legal basis of the brigade rules of 1984. This introduction sets out the basis for their creation and their purpose. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we can see in the first couple of paragraphs, it says they are based on the concept of the All People's Defence; the strategy of arms struggle; the NOR experiences; experiences drawn from exercises of units, commands and staff, so on and so forth. And then in the second paragraph it says: "Considering differences in terms of organisation and establishment structure and the purpose and possibility of various types of brigade in the infantry, it is necessary to apply the provisions of these rules creatively and according to the concrete conditions for the preparation, organisation, and conduct of combat operations and the actual combat capability of each individual brigade." And then going, you can't see this because I think it's on your next page, but going down one, two, three, four -- five paragraphs, it says: "The aim of the rules is to ensure that each separate brigade according to its purpose and capabilities adopt and apply unified views, attitudes, and tactical moves in the preparation, organisation, and execution of combat operations in All People's Defence war. It is a duty of all senior staff and commands to study the provisions of these rules in detail and to test and evaluate them during training for all types of brigades and for the conditions for which they operate. The rules are intended for the training of commands, staffs, units, institutions, army cadets, and students at the military schools, as well as the reserve senior staff."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I am very sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Put in simple terms, this document created pursuant to an instruction is a training manual, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It has a slightly broader purpose than just a training manual. As I said initially, it has a broader purpose somewhat because training involves a number of processes. First you have the actual schooling process, then you have training which involves daily work and education, then you have training in terms of applying experiences, as also referred to by these rules. These are rules which are intended for training, but they are also intended to ensure the adherence of certain principles and a creative endeavour in keeping with particular situations and needs. In that sense it is more broad than just training.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would "guidance" be a better word?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on now to another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And it's 7D717. And I want to start, please -- well, I just want to look at B/C/S at page 6, and English, page 2. It might actually be helpful if in the B/C/S before we show the witness page 6, we show him the first page so he can see what the rules are, which ironically is page -- yes, we've got it there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Kosovac, you were able to see what this set of rules were by looking at the front page, were you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want you now to look at clause 17 which is in precisely similar terms to another provision you looked at earlier this morning which you were being asked questions by Mr. Krgovic. But Article 17 says: "In the absence of the commander, the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander stand in for him with all the commander's rights and duties." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see Article 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the word used in Serbian for "standing in for" is "zastupa" [phoen] rather than anything else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And is that your understanding of the legal position of the Chief of Staff within a brigade of the Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. In terms of its character, these rules are a binding documents in contrast with the previous rules which had a quite different purpose. However, these rules are also binding upon the commander as well as upon the Chief of Staff. What does Article 17 say? Article 17 has divested the commander of the right to appoint anyone else from his -- from among his subordinates to stand in for him, but it stipulates that it is exclusively the Chief of Staff that can stand in for him. However, it is generally known that standing in here is also an obligation which also needs to be regulated by an order to that effect. Without such an order there can be no standing in and there can be no rights or obligations stemming from such a position, a standing-in position, according to these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can that be a permanent order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Both the Law on the Army and the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska were very precise to the effect that standing in is limited in terms of duration. According to the law that substitution, that standing in can last for a maximum of six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've pre-empted my last question on this topic, which is to look at page 3 of that document which is not translated. So you will have to help us, General. Above the title of the rules you can see the authority, and as you've already told us, this is a document which has the authority of law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a binding document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to move away from the Rules of the Army of Yugoslavia and turn to the Army of Republika Srpska. And I'd like you, please, to consider P26. To be quite frank, General, I can't recall whether you did consider this document in preparation of your report. Have you seen it before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. No, no, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, would you take a few moments just to read it through.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now having seen the content, I think -- no, I know that I have seen this document before but I have not cited it in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I thought you probably had. This is effectively the document that creates the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which requires of commanders their proposals for creating the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska. So these are -- this is eliciting proposals for the creation of the structure of the Republika Srpska Army, and some parameters are given to the effect that the proponents giving such proposals must explain their proposals for the structure of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And by the parameters do you mean the section in the document that says that: "The Army of Republika Srpska should be an army consisting of quick, mobile and efficient units based on current establishment formations, existing combat hardware, weapons, and other military equipment, light infantry brigades are to be the preferred options ..." And then: "Existing divisions shall be abandoned as organisational units." Are those the parameters that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes absolutely. These are parameters which are of the essence for making proposal -- for proposing a structure of the army. As well as this where it says that the army has to be capable of -- of offensive defence and the use of other hardware. This is the different modules, capability, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that those parameters made the Army of Republika Srpska, in structural terms, a rather different animal to the Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely agree because one substantial parameter is organisation, which is why specific organs are set up to deal with organisation, in order to avoid stereotype and in order to make the optimum organisational structure in keeping with the objectives, the available personnel, and the available hardware, in order to make an observation which will develop very quickly if you obtain different hardware and other means of combat, as well as different personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We are moving on very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we now have P417 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And again, General Kosovac, I am just going to show you the first page of this document to see whether it is familiar to you, that you've read it either in preparation of your report or in preparation for your evidence or at any other time. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cited some of his elements in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good. And just to explain why I'm having to do this, you and I haven't had the opportunity of discussing what evidence you are going to give today, have we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You and me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, you and me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we now please go to page 10 of that document in B/C/S and in English, please. And I'm concerned with Articles 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if you don't mind, I am going to deal with them in reverse order. We will start with Article 17, if we may. Firstly, a general question about these provisional service regulations for the Army of Republika Srpska. They were written about three months after the document we've just been looking at, the invitation for proposals as to the structure of the army. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the service regulations also have a different purpose, the interim one. These provisional service rules on the Army of Republika Srpska define precisely the competencies and the relationships between the unit commands and the senior officers, the commanding officers, and this -- actually this chapter is called and deals with relations in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And you are familiar with the whole document, I don't want to take you through it, but they do not, do they, expressly incorporate any rules from the Yugoslav National Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are self-sufficient, as it were, but it is obvious that it was created on the basis of the Rules of Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, if we go to Article 17, that creates an obligation to carry out the orders of a superior officer. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 17, yes, it speaks about the superior commander or the superior commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most senior one and the superior one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've again answered my next question. It's in two parts. It defines to an extent who the superior officer is if the obvious superior is not present. It's the most senior officer present; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I did not quite understand your question. Would you be so kind as to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I was just looking at the second paragraph of Article 17 which reads: "Members of the army shall carry out the orders of the most senior officer present when the superior officer is absent."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to Article 16, but first I want to see if you agree with this general proposition. A commanding officer is not necessarily a commander, is he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does that mean that you agree with what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that is particularly the case when we consider the giving of orders in relation to a joint task, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I did not understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that is my fault. Let's consider a joint task which is specifically legislated for in Article 16. We have a classic example of a joint task in this case. Operation Krivaja 95 was a joint task, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was precise. Operation Krivaja 95 does not exist. There were active combat actions which were conducted under covert name or secret name Krivaja 95. An operation -- if you want to call this an operation, that would mean that you are trying to put documents somewhere in something that actually never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Let's try and take another example. A joint task could be ordered which involved a unit from one brigade, a unit from a second brigade, a unit from the corps, and a unit from the Main Staff. That would be a joint task, wouldn't it, where units from four other units combine together to perform a task?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, and the question and answer to it has two tiers. It is good that you took an order which regulates active combat and the example you provided is also good. If a command unites the activities of several units, then that command is also in command of those units and the person that that command appoints, which we illustrated several times last week. This Article 16 or bullet point 16 is something that happens in a different situation. If for any reason a connection is interrupted with a command, then these units that you listed will still be one whole and they will act as one whole, and the senior officer assumes the role of the superior commander and regulates all the activities for as long as they last.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think you have answered my question. The senior officer would be in command of all those disparate units that were combined together performing the same task, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If they are on a joint task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the commanders of all the units from which those units originally came would not be in command of them. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officer who would be in command of the task would be also in command of that whole consisting of three or four units, and every commander or senior officer leading their respective units would be carrying out orders. A system of hierarchy would soon be established in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I am now confident that you have answered my question, and I'm content with that answer. There is just one last matter I want to ask you about, and it involves a further document which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like you to look please at B/C/S page 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And those of us who speak English can look at page 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like you just quickly to consider point 65 in relation to some questions you answered from Mr. Bourgon the other day. And do you agree with the provision of Article 65 that the operational duty at the command post is organised by the Chief of Staff of the unit?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: General Kosovac, thank you very much. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. That brings us to you, Mr. Vanderpuye, but the break is with us. Shall we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you wish, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you still estimate eight hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, it's substantially reduced from that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and Your Honours. Good afternoon to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, General. My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution I am going to put some questions to you in relation to your direct examination and also your cross-examination, as well as your expert report. Since we don't speak the same language, I will try to go a little bit slow, and I would appreciate it if you could also respond slowly so that there is time for an adequate translation or accurate translation of what we say to one another for the record. If you have any questions about what I ask you, please just let me know and I'll try to rephrase it in a way that we can best understand one another more clearly. Now, you were put some questions --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Thank you very much, I understand perfectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Great. You were put some questions -- some questions you put to you, rather, by my colleague Mr. Krgovic with respect to the testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Dragomir Keserovic, and he asked you in particular some questions regarding Mr. Keserovic's statements concerning General Miletic on page 32 of the transcript. What I wanted to do is read to you what he said before the questions that were put to you by my colleague, and let me refer you -- or from my colleagues, rather, to the trial transcript. It's at page 31 and begins at line 22 and it reads as follows: "Q. Do you know was there an acting Chief of Staff, deputy commander, in Han Pijesak while Milovanovic was away?" "A. I don't know if there was one officially. If you allow me, may I say that --" "Q. It's pretty simple, but go ahead, go ahead. No, go ahead. If you need to explain, you can always explain." "A. I meant to say, that -- and you probably have this information anyway, that the Main Staff involved such a small number of people that quite literally everybody did everything. So people could be replaced all the time. If one person was not there then somebody else would -- somebody else could take over for him. And people would have several duties. So it is possible that from that point of view somebody did stand in for General Milovanovic, but I am not sure of whether anybody was officially appointed." He then goes on, as was brought out by my colleague, to say that General Miletic would be the number 3 man on the staff. So let me ask you this, General: Is it possible, in your estimation, your experience, that Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic arrived at the conclusion that General Miletic was number 3 in the staff because he had the opportunity to see General Miletic's signature as standing in for the Chief of Staff on a number of occasions, given his experience as a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is possible that Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, who I don't want to deny any capabilities in his part of the profession, gained that impression for several reasons. One of the reason may be that people often mistake the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska with the staff of Republika Srpska. The second reason may be that the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska is often mistaken for a command post. And the third reason may be that very often, based on personal impression, one is tempted to give an evaluation. And fourthly, it is generally known that most of the officers, not only in the Army of Republika Srpska but also the other militaries that I am aware of, the problem of organisational establishment and personnel affairs is the least known and no simple logic can be applied to it. And this is also indicated by the use of the word "standing in for," "VD," acting for, which never existed in the army. It does not exist in any military. This "VD," acting on behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, what he describes in his testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first reason given by the witness, I am not sure whether it was correctly translated. I will read it again and, General, could you confirm whether it was what you said: "One of the reason may be is that people often mistake the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska with the staff of Republika Srpska." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that people often mistook the staff of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska for the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic describes appears to be regular regularity of unofficial assignments of duties and responsibilities within the Main Staff. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me, I believe that the prevailing fact here is the fact that he was often in contact with the basic command post, and the person he often -- most often saw there was General Miletic. And at one point General Miletic represented a focal point for him and everything resolved around him. And the fact is that General Miletic was almost exclusively at the command post. He rarely toured the units, and when he was absent it would be to visit his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think I will move ahead. I will probably come back to this in a little bit. Let me ask you some more general background questions. First, can you tell us, do you have any practical experience in terms of commanding combat operations, whether it be strategically directed, operationally, or tactically?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us when and where that was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was bombarded, I represented the chief of the third administration of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska which organised work outside of the system of the command post because that administration was duty-bound to contact -- maintain contacts with the government, the ministries, and other organisations and the military. Very often as the chief of that administration, I cooperated with the command posts, almost all of them, and I also toured my military territorial units which were deployed across the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. And I take it that you've had experience preparing technical reports of the type and nature that you've presented here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see in my CV the works that I authored and the expert report of this nature is the only such report that I've prepared. However, on the part of the Tribunal I was also engaged as a military expert in the Perisic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So this is the first military or technical military expert report you've prepared, at least for court. That's fair to say, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is my first encounter with any court or the judiciary system as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you produced a report or are you in the process of producing the report with respect to your Perisic engagement?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It -- the preparations are underway. Once I am done with this, the Perisic case will become one of my focal tasks, in addition to my everyday duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You recognise, of course, given your experience, that in preparing a report, particularly a technical report such as this, you have to be analytical, right, in your review of both materials and the facts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely clear on that. In the introductory part of my report I emphasized that and I also emphasized what methods I used, and I particularly explained how and why I used the method of modelling, or the modelling method.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I asked you that because I believe it was on Friday you testified that you didn't try to put together all the pieces of the puzzle. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like you to be more precise because in some instances that sentence could be -- can be excellent and in some others it could be disastrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question, then, to you directly. Is it the case that you tried to put all the pieces of the puzzle together or not?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of my expert report I tried to complete the mosaic, and that's why I searched for some comparisons where I did not have any documents available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In preparing your report you tried to be thorough. That's fair to say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that anything else would be disastrous and would not comply with the task and the topic. An officer, an expert of my rank and reputation would not embark on any task in any different way. They wouldn't be superficial. They would not leave any stones unturned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so in preparing this report you tried to be neutral and objective; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've just asked me, this is the starting point of my expert report. I perceive myself as an expert, a military expert that was engaged by the Tribunal and the topic was given to me by the Miletic Defence. In that sense, when it comes to the functioning of experts, at the end of my testimony I am going to provide some proposals to the Trial Chamber irrespective of the fact whether they will be inclined to adopt my proposals or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood you, but do you mean that in terms of your report or in terms of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the place and the role of an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in order to accomplish all these things, to be analytical and thorough and neutral and objective in the course of preparing this report, you, as an expert, know that among other things you have to be critical or you have to critically at least evaluate the nature and the applicability of the information that you consider in preparing the report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. This does ring a bell. I am very familiar with all these concepts. That's why I can tell you that my effort has not been in vain. Unlike any other expert reports, I did not want to analyse one military party to the conflict without obtaining a number of documents originating from the other army in the conflict. I even researched documents that concerned other militaries outside of the former Yugoslavia, and that's why whenever I say that other militaries used the same thing, that means that I had direct access to the information pertaining to such other militaries and I studied them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I asked the question in relation to some of the answers that you gave my colleagues when they questioned you as well, and in particular, in relation to your acknowledgment, upon questioning by my colleague Mr. Haynes, that there is a vast body of regulatory documents from the former Yugoslavia that may be applicable to any given circumstance concerning the VRS. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is affirmative. That is the case indeed. However, I need to provide an adequate comment in respect of this answer. All the militaries that originated from the former JNA, among their command cadre or among the top management as it were had officers from the former JNA, and it is only natural that all the command activities were taken over from the JNA. There was another comparative advantage which you yourself could observe in the courtroom. A large number of the documents issued by the JNA were drafted in the languages of the various peoples, so none of them had to be translated. And the most important thing of all, the officers in question had been trained to use the documents in question. At the beginning, the laws were drafted by adopting the existing laws with some minor changes. As the time went on, the different countries incorporated their own idiosyncrasies and their own features into such laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So I take it you took into consideration the degree of binding nature of any given law, regulation, instruction, in terms of arriving at your conclusions when you were developing your report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I take it you also considered the fact that many of these rules, regulations, and instructions were creatively applied, both in the former JNA -- or, rather, in the JNA and in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was very precise in my expert report as well as in my words uttered here before the Trial Chamber, and I was really very precise in defining the creative application, the binding application. And also when I explained the specific features of the two sets of documents I was very careful and I very often emphasized that, and I am always prepared to make a distinction between one and the other thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your report you identify the information that you relied upon in reaching your conclusions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to the information I used. I didn't provide an exhaustive list of the information because it never is final and exhaustive. So over the last few days I came across certain information that I hadn't previously seen. I was precise when I said that the expert report is not final. It can always be amended on the basis of new information obtained, and I am quite prepared to engage in a professional discussion with regard to this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. The documents that you relied on in preparing this report you received primarily from the Miletic Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say so. Because I can see that an expert in the court doesn't have access to the database, I mostly used documents that the Defence provided me with. I used documents that I came across, too. I read expert reports, other reports. I read through transcripts of conversations that were held, and I spoke to many people who were directly or indirectly involved in anything that was of interest to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, that's what I want to get to, actually, because you mentioned on a number of occasions during your testimony that you spoke to very numerous high-ranking officials in various armed forces in respect of your engagement. So could you please tell us who it is that you spoke to concerning the preparation of the report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I incorporated into the report does not only concern individuals or generals or people who were involved in this field, people that I spoke to directly with. It also concerns people or individuals whose documents I used. And among other things, I most frequently spoke to individuals involved in field of activity like my own, that concerned the organisation and functioning of a system. With regard to certain elements of the organisation and function of a system, I spoke about such elements to General Simic. He has testified here, and I spoke to him while he was still a Chief of the Main Staff of the VRS -- or, rather, while he was still in that position, I officially visited him in Banja Luka, and I then I spoke with him because I was interested in some of his experiences. As for General Skrbic, I spoke to him when he came to visit the Army of Yugoslavia. When he did so, he worked in the sector where my organisational unit was based. I spoke to numerous colonels at various conferences and I established contact with them. There were a lot of people I spoke to directly or indirectly. I don't want to offend anyone by saying that I didn't speak to such and such a person; however, when the decision was taken to draft this report -- or, as of that moment I didn't contact any of these individuals because I wanted to work on the basis of the information I had already obtained and I wanted this report to be an original work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Are you saying that you -- excuse me, you didn't speak to either General Simic or Skrbic after you were engaged to prepare the report? Because that's how it reads in the transcript. I am wondering if whether there is an error?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what it says, there is an error. I didn't speak to them about the report after I started working on the report. I was very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase my question and maybe I can be a little bit more precise. Did you speak to them in relation to the preparation of your report at any point during that process?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were very precise at the beginning and I answered that precise question. With regard to drafting the report, well, I didn't speak to anyone about it because I wanted it to be my own original work, but I spoke to a huge variety of individuals with regard to their experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- I suppose what's troubling me a little bit, I would like to know if you could, more precisely, when you say "huge numbers of individuals" who you are talking about, and you've mentioned two people. Could you be a little bit more precise about who it is you spoke to and what you spoke to them about, because your report covers a broad area of material.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be more precise I'd -- well, I would have to remember the list of individuals about whom I spoke to about all these matters. Up until the end of 1995, I was the executive director of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia and Montenegro, or, rather, of Serbia. Prior to that I was the assistant or, rather, deputy minister for human affairs, personnel affairs. The subject of this work that was drafted was the subject of each and every conversation I had with each individual, each official who worked in the system. With regard to organisational matters, I spoke to a NATO officer about this. I also spoke about organisation to individuals in the Pentagon, to people from the Ministry of Defence. I spoke about this to the G5 head. As far as organisation is concerned, I spoke to officers from the Slovenian army. As far as organisation is concerned, I spoke to officers from the Slovak army. I also spoke to officers from the VRS about organisational matters. I spoke about organisational matters to former JNA officers who were involved in this area. I had presentations at conferences. I am a member of the Atlantic Council of Serbia. I am a member of the administration of the Atlantic counsel, and to this very day I speak to these people about all aspects that concern organisation, functioning, and command. If you are interested in any specific names, well, I provided you with two names that are fresh in your memory, but I can look into other names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have had the opportunity to look at your report, and it is really quite sophisticated so forgive me if I err with respect to some of its content, but I did not see in your report any mention of any interviews that you had with anybody concerning any of the conclusions that you've drawn. I don't believe your report contains any footnotes with respect to individuals that you had these conversations with, and I am wondering why that is. So if you could tell us why is it that your report doesn't reflect the fact that you spoke to such a wide array of highly qualified individuals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for saying that the report is sophisticated. It's an honour for me to hear it described in this way. I must say that when I started working on this report, a very limited period of time was used to draft the report. In fact, I relied on material used by other investigators or drafted by other investigators and I wanted to reconstruct the way in which the VRS was organised and mobilized. However, the working method itself requires a lot of time, the use of a lot of associates, many things have to be verified, and it wasn't possible for me to draft it in this way. However, given that I spoke to many individuals and worked in this manner, well, all these factors were incorporated in my CV in the description of the duties that I performed. These are elements that I used for the report. As I didn't conduct any specific interviews when I started drafting the report, I didn't contact anyone in particular, and as a result, I didn't want to mention any names because there was no basis for referring to such names at such a point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Bear with me for a moment. On the 12th of this month when you testified, and this is at page 2991, you were testifying in relation to a question that my colleague put to you concerning General Miletic's rank and order. And on line 13, during the course of your answer you said: "Reading the documents linked to this case, I have seen that very often there was a lot of confusion about what commanding officer in the Army of Republika Srpska held what rank. Bearing in mind that they had an order on the operation of the Army of Republika Srpska, that they also had the establishment, that I had a large number of orders, I contacted additional interviews with those officers who dealt with organisation within the Army of Republika Srpska and established on the basis of all this the precise rank and order in the Army of Republika Srpska." Having read that to you, I put my question to you again as to whom it is that you contacted after you were engaged to prepare this report. Did you contact anyone after you started this report or after you were engaged by the Miletic Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything has fallen into place in your question, but confusion doesn't make sense because it's not a word I use very often, but I think I have understood your question and I'll try and be precise again. When I was drafting this report, I did not speak to anyone for the purposes of drafting the report, but when I did speak to people I spoke to them to find out how they worked, what tasks they carried out, and what sort of problems they encountered and that is why my intention was to reconstruct the way in which matters were organised. In my opinion, someone else should have done this, not this expert, but time did not allow for this. When there were certain problems that I encountered, when it was difficult to understand certain things, I would contact, for example, General Skrbic, and I would ask him about some elements of an order. I would ask him, for example, whether an order on standing in for other officers was drafted. He said that no such order at that highest level had been drafted. I didn't tell Skrbic that I would use this in the report or not or anything of the kind. I would ask about how many problems they had with establishment. I asked about how establishment was dealt with. I asked Colonel Kovacevic about this. He said that they followed the system they had and relied on the basis -- on the documents that the army had. I don't know if I can find a document about organisation or if I didn't know how to find such a document -- well, he didn't know anything about it, he said that he wasn't part of the system, he hadn't been for a long time, and he said he knew nothing about it. Perhaps the problem is that you have something concealed within your question and, as a result, I don't understand it, but I am being very precise and I have repeated it a number of times. As far as the report is concerned, not a single sentence was added from someone's interview, for example, and therefore no references were made. Given the tasks that I had to perform and the context I established, well, this was the base upon which I drafted this expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At page 29992 of the transcript, you go on to describe your diagram, and you say: "Based on all this I reach the conclusion presented here. I have checked this diagram with a large number of officers engaged in organisational work, and they all agreed with every detail of this diagram." Do you remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That you had checked the diagram that you developed in relation to representing the rank and order in the Republika Srpska with a number of individuals that were engaged in organisational work. I am referring just to the 12th of January during the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this mean that you are referring to figure number 14?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe I am, but you correct me if I am wrong. I am only referring to the subject of your testimony, in particular that you said that you checked the diagram with a number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there is an interpretation issue. I went through my report very rapidly, but there aren't any diagrams. There are only figures. There are various figures, but if you're talking about rank and order that would correspond to figure 14. And it's correct that in figure 14 -- or, rather, with regard -- I spoke to a number of people about figure 14, but it's not as if I provided these people with figure 14 and then had them verify it, or I spoke to them about the working method used. And since this question was often put about this being my own work, well, during the break it occurred to me that there is a document in the army, it's a JNA document that's been adopted by the Army of Yugoslavia, and I know that it was worked on by the VRS. And I know that they established some kind of an organisation on the basis of that document in the army of Slovenia, but the document hasn't been referred to, but the document is called "Instructions for Drafting Mobilization Plan Documents." I am convinced that this document also exists in the database you have here and that we could have a look at it and work with it, but it's one of the documents that also speaks about the issue of rank. It's important because you can see that rank and order aren't concepts that I have invented here. As to the method on how one obtained rank and order, well, about these methods I spoke to, for example, military officials, former ones, present ones. I asked them whether they had any experience about rank and order in foreign armies --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... concerned about whether or not you presented this figure or diagram to anybody after you had prepared it. And so I think you have probably answered my question just fine. If the Court would like, we could break, but I could continue also for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have got two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- the next two minutes if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, I take it that you have prepared quite extensively for your testimony before coming here, right? You could probably answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't seem to be someone who is not very serious to you. Yes, I prepared very thoroughly for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you met with both the Miletic Defence team and the Gvero Defence team; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you failed to mention someone. I also met or spoke to Ms. Nikolic, and that's been said in the courtroom. We met and spoke for an hour or two about certain main issues, and I did not meet with anyone else nor did I speak to anyone else before my testimony here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How long did you meet with the Gvero team for, if you could tell us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KOSOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am afraid I couldn't really say, but if I said it was between one and two hours, well, I think that that's probably a fairly precise estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We will stop here. We will continue tomorrow. Do you think you will finish tomorrow or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am hoping to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are hoping to. Mr. Haynes, please note.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Obviously, I think there will be some kind of redirect later on, but on the assumption that we might finish tomorrow or latest Wednesday, be prepared. Yes, yes. Incidentally, Judge Prost is reminding me, you have to come back to us on Kovacevic and whether you have any other --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are aware that we need to make a final decision about that and to relay that to the Trial Chamber and also the parties, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And I am grateful to Judge Prost for mentioning that at this stage. As well that, Your Honours, we do wish to make this opening statement as well which will take up a session, approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have -- Mr. Thayer is trying to determine whether he needs to get ready for this witness, so if we could get that information as soon as possible. We also wonder if there is no evidence, what kind of an opening statement that would be. That would be a closing statement. So if there is no evidence, I don't see that an opening statement, well, fits the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I deal with the first point. I have repeatedly told Mr. Thayer that he needs to be prepared to deal with our expert. I have said that to him ten times at least, and that is the answer to the question that my learned friend Mr. McCloskey --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- poses. Mr. Thayer needs to be prepared for it. Secondly, so far as the other issue is concerned, clearly that is something if we call no evidence that my learned friend is entitled to address --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- and you'll need to hear argument about and then resolve. Now is not the time to do that, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree. I agree. We will continue tomorrow at 9.00 -- tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.48 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
